title: Self-Regulatory Organizations; Nasdaq PHLX LLC; Notice of Filing and Immediate Effectiveness of a Proposed Rule Change To Amend the Exchange's Transaction Fees at Equity 7, Section 3
raw_text:
Self-Regulatory Organizations; Nasdaq PHLX LLC; Notice of Filing and Immediate Effectiveness of a Proposed Rule Change To Amend the Exchange's Transaction Fees at Equity 7, Section 3

1. Purpose The purpose of the proposed rule change is to amend the Exchange's transaction fees at PHLX Equity 7, Section 3. The Exchange proposes to streamline its schedule of credits to member organizations providing displayed liquidity on Nasdaq PSX, and to eliminate the supplemental credit to member organizations providing displayed liquidity on Nasdaq PSX . First Change Currently, the Exchange pays a credit to a member organization that provides liquidity on Nasdaq PSX through displayed quotes/orders. This credit currently has four separate tiers. The tiers are not labeled in the rule text, but this filing will refer to them as Tier 1 through Tier 4: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ------------------------------------------------------------------------ Tier 4............................... $0.0033 per share executed for Quotes/Orders entered by a member organization that provides 0.15% or more of total Consolidated Volume during the month. Tier 3............................... $0.0032 per share executed for Quotes/Orders entered by a member organization that provides 0.07% or more of total Consolidated Volume during the month. Tier 2............................... $0.0030 per share executed for Quotes/Orders entered by a member organization that provides 0.05% or more of total Consolidated Volume during the month. Tier 1............................... $0.0020 per share executed for all other Quotes/Orders. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ The Exchange proposes to eliminate Tiers 2, 3, and 4. Therefore, the Exchange would pay a member organization providing displayed liquidity on Nasdaq PSX a credit of $0.0020 per share executed for displayed quotes/orders entered by a member organization--regardless of how much volume the member organization provides during the month. Second Change The Exchange currently pays a supplemental credit to a member organization that provides liquidity on Nasdaq PSX through displayed quotes/orders. This is a supplemental credit of $0.00005 per share executed for displayed quotes/orders entered by a member organization that: (i) provides 0.10% or more of total Consolidated Volume during the prior month; and (ii) provides 0.10% or more of total Consolidated Volume during the month. The Exchange proposes to eliminate this supplemental credit. 2. Statutory Basis The Exchange believes that its proposal is consistent with Section 6(b) of the Act, in general, and furthers the objectives of Sections 6(b)(4) and 6(b)(5) of the Act, in particular, in that it provides for the equitable allocation of reasonable dues, fees and other charges among members and issuers and other persons using any facility, and is not designed to permit unfair discrimination between customers, issuers, brokers, or dealers. The Exchange's proposed changes to its schedule of credits are reasonable in several respects. As a threshold matter, the Exchange is subject to significant competitive forces in the market for equity securities transaction services that constrain its pricing determinations in that market. The fact that this market is competitive has long been recognized by the courts. In NetCoalition v. Securities and Exchange Commission, the D.C. Circuit stated as follows: ``[n]o one disputes that competition for order flow is `fierce.' . . . As the SEC explained, `[i]n the U.S. national market system, buyers and sellers of securities, and the broker-dealers that act as their order-routing agents, have a wide range of choices of where to route orders for execution'; [and] `no exchange can afford to take its market share percentages for granted' because `no exchange possesses a monopoly, regulatory or otherwise, in the execution of order flow from broker dealers'. . . .'' The Commission and the courts have repeatedly expressed their preference for competition over regulatory intervention in determining prices, products, and services in the securities markets. In Regulation NMS, while adopting a series of steps to improve the current market model, the Commission highlighted the importance of market forces in determining prices and SRO revenues and, also, recognized that current regulation of the market system ``has been remarkably successful in promoting market competition in its broader forms that are most important to investors and listed companies.'' Numerous indicia demonstrate the competitive nature of this market. For example, clear substitutes to the Exchange exist in the market for equity security transaction services. The Exchange is only one of several equity venues to which market participants may direct their order flow. Competing equity exchanges offer similar tiered pricing structures to that of the Exchange, including schedules of rebates and fees that apply based upon members achieving certain volume thresholds. Within this environment, market participants can freely and often do shift their order flow among the Exchange and competing venues in response to changes in their respective pricing schedules. As such, the proposal reflects the Exchange's ongoing assessment of how to allocate its limited incentive resources in a competitive market and how to maintain a schedule of credits that is understandable and administrable for member organizations. First Change The Exchange believes that eliminating the three volume-based displayed liquidity credit tiers and retaining the existing $0.0020 per share executed credit for all displayed Quotes/Orders is reasonable because it will streamline the schedule and make the applicable credit easier for member organizations to understand and apply. The Exchange has limited resources to devote to incentive programs, and it is appropriate for the Exchange to periodically reallocate those incentives in a manner that best achieves its overall mix of objectives. title: Self-Regulatory Organizations; KalshiEX LLC; Notice of Filing and Immediate Effectiveness of a Proposed Rule Change Relating to Listing Standards for Security Futures Products
raw_text:
Self-Regulatory Organizations; KalshiEX LLC; Notice of Filing and Immediate Effectiveness of a Proposed Rule Change Relating to Listing Standards for Security Futures Products

1. Purpose Kalshi is registered with the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (``CFTC'') as a designated contract market (``DCM'') under the Commodity Exchange Act (``CEA'') and notice-registered with the Commission as a national securities exchange for security futures products pursuant to the notice registration provisions of Section 6(g) of the Act. Under its notice-registration, Kalshi lists as security futures cash-settled contracts that convey exposure to the price of an underlying equity security, have no pre-specified expiration date and are designated as Perpetual SFPs in their respective contract specifications, pursuant to listing standard rules for security futures products that it has adopted under a separate rule filing under Section 19(b)(7) of the Act and Rule 19b-7 thereunder filed on September 18, 2026. In light of anticipated trading interest, Kalshi plans to reduce the time to market for the listing and trading of Perpetual SFPs on certain covered securities following their initial public offering (``IPO''). To effect this plan, Kalshi proposes to adopt certain rule changes to the introductory language in Rule 14.3 and Rules 14.3(c) and 14.3(d) of Chapter 14 of the Kalshi Rulebook. Description of Proposed Rule Change Rule 14.3 of Kalshi's Rulebook sets forth the initial listing eligibility criteria for Underlying Securities of Perpetual SFPs listed on the Exchange. Rule 14.3 requires that an Underlying Security that is common stock satisfy several criteria at the time of initial listing in order to be eligible for a Perpetual SFP on the Exchange, including that the Underlying Security must (i) pursuant to Rule 14.3(a), be registered and listed on a U.S. national securities exchange and must be an ``NMS security'' as defined in Section 11A of the Exchange Act and Rule 600(b) of SEC Regulation NMS, (ii) pursuant to Rule 14.3(b), have a market capitalization of not less than $100,000,000,000 (one hundred billion U.S. dollars), (iii) pursuant to Rule 14.3(c), have an average daily value of transactions (``ADTV'') of not less than $450,000,000 (four hundred and fifty million U.S. dollars) over the six months immediately preceding the New Product Committee's review, except where the Underlying Security has been listed for trading for less than six months, in which case the Underlying Security must have an ADTV of not less than $1,000,000,000 (one billion U.S. dollars) over the prior month, (iv) pursuant to Rule 14.3(d), if the Underlying Security is a ``covered security'' as defined in Section 18(b)(1)(A) of the Securities Act of 1933, have had a closing price of at least $3.00 for the previous five consecutive business days preceding the listing of a Perpetual SFP on such Underlying Security (or a closing price of at least $7.50 for the same period if the Underlying Security is not a ``covered security''), (v) pursuant to Rule 14.3(e), have a public float of not less than 7,000,000 (seven million) shares, (vi) pursuant to Rule 14.3(f), have an estimated deliverable supply in excess of 20,000,000 (twenty million) shares, (vii) pursuant to Rule 14.3(g), have an issuer that is current in all periodic reporting obligations under Sections 13 or 15(d) of the Act, and (viii) pursuant to Rule 14.3(j), have at least 2,000 security holders (whether of record or beneficial). The initial eligibility criterion regarding trading volume history of potential Underlying Securities in Rule 14.3(c) is framed in terms of ADTV over the prior month, so does not contemplate Underlying Securities with exchange-trading histories of less than one month. Accordingly, under the current rule, if an IPO occurs on a given day, the earliest date that the Exchange could list a Perpetual SFP on such security would be one month following such date. The Exchange therefore proposes to amend Rule 14.3(c) to provide that, ``where the Underlying Security has been listed for trading for less than one month, . . . the Underlying Security must have had a trading volume (in all markets in which it is traded) of at least 2,400,000 shares since the Underlying Security's initial public offering day.'' The Exchange also proposes to include a definition of ``initial public offering day'' in the introductory language in Rule 14.3, which would define ``initial public offering day'' of an Underlying Security as ``the first day on which the Underlying Security trades `regular way' on a national securities exchange.'' As proposed, this rule change would permit the Exchange to list a Perpetual SFP on an Underlying Security with a trading volume of 2,400,000 shares since its IPO, regardless of the length of time between the IPO and the New Product Committee's review of the Underlying Security, subject to satisfaction of all other initial eligibility criteria in Rule 14.3, as amended herein. This proposed amendment is consistent with the trading volume criteria adopted by securities options exchanges with respect to the eligibility criteria for underlying securities of securities options, which require such underlying securities to have had a total trading volume of 2,400,000 shares in the preceding twelve months without specifying a monthly ADTV requirement or any minimum lookback period. Additionally, the minimum share price criterion in Rule 14.3(d) requires the market price per share of an underlying covered security to have been at least $3.00 for the previous five consecutive business days preceding the date on which the Exchange commences to list and trade a Perpetual SFP on such Underlying Security (the ``five-day lookback period''). Under the current rule, even assuming adoption of the proposed amendment to Rule 14.3(c) discussed above, if an IPO occurs on a Monday, the earliest date the Exchange could list a Perpetual SFP on the relevant security would be the following Monday, with the market price determined by the closing price over the five-day lookback period from the Monday of the IPO through the following Friday.

title: Self-Regulatory Organizations; Nasdaq PHLX LLC; Notice of Filing and Immediate Effectiveness of a Proposal To Amend Equity 4 To Remove All References to the CORE FIX Order Entry Protocol
raw_text:
Self-Regulatory Organizations; Nasdaq PHLX LLC; Notice of Filing and Immediate Effectiveness of a Proposal To Amend Equity 4 To Remove All References to the CORE FIX Order Entry Protocol

1. Purpose In September 2025 the Exchange added CORE FIX to its rulebook in Equity 4, in anticipation of making this new order entry protocol available to Exchange Participants in October of 2025. In December 2025 the Exchange extended the implementation date for CORE FIX to the first quarter of 2026. In March 2026 the Exchange extended the implementation date for CORE FIX to the end of 2026. In spite of its best efforts, the Exchange has been unable to generate interest in CORE FIX among Exchange Participants. Therefore, rather than deploy an order entry protocol that Participants are not even interested in testing, the Exchange proposes to abandon its plans to deploy CORE FIX. This will allow the Exchange to better allocate its technological development resources. The Exchange notes that it will continue to offer all the order entry protocols that are currently available and operative on the Exchange--namely, OUCH, RASH, FLITE, and FIX. The Exchange proposes to eliminate all references to CORE FIX that are currently present in Equity 4. Specifically, these references are found in Rules 3100 (Limit Up-Limit Down Plan and Trading Halts on PSX), 3301A (Order Types), 3301B (Order Attributes), and 3307 (Processing of Orders). 2. Statutory Basis The Exchange believes that its proposal is consistent with Section 6(b) of the Act, in general, and furthers the objectives of Section 6(b)(5) of the Act, in particular, in that it is designed to promote just and equitable principles of trade, to remove impediments to and perfect the mechanism of a free and open market and a national market system, and, in general to protect investors and the public interest. The Exchange believes that the proposed rule change is designed to promote just and equitable principles of trade because it will ensure that the Exchange's rulebook accurately reflects the order entry protocols that are available and operative on the Exchange. Removing references to CORE FIX, which the Exchange will not deploy, will avoid confusion among Participants and other market participants regarding the protocols available for order entry. The proposed rule change will not alter the operation of the Exchange's market, the treatment of orders, or the rights or obligations of Participants; the Exchange will continue to offer the OUCH, RASH, FLITE, and FIX protocols. Accordingly, the proposal will remove impediments to and perfect the mechanism of a free and open market and a national market system, and will protect investors and the public interest by providing clear and accurate information concerning the Exchange's order entry protocols. B. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Burden on Competition The Exchange does not believe that the proposed rule change will impose any burden on competition not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. The proposed rule change is not designed to address any competitive issue; instead, its purpose is to ensure that the Exchange's rulebook accurately reflects the protocols that are available and operative on the Exchange. Removing references to CORE FIX will not deprive any Participant of an available order entry protocol, because CORE FIX has not been deployed on the Exchange. Participants will continue to be able to choose among the OUCH, RASH, FLITE, and FIX protocols based on their trading needs. Accordingly, the proposal will not impose any burden on competition, either among Exchange Participants or between the Exchange and other trading venues. C. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Comments on the Proposed Rule Change Received From Members, Participants, or Others No written comments were either solicited or received. III. Date of Effectiveness of the Proposed Rule Change and Timing for Commission Action Because the foregoing proposed rule change does not: (i) significantly affect the protection of investors or the public interest; (ii) impose any significant burden on competition; and (iii) become operative for 30 days from the date on which it was filed, or such shorter time as the Commission may designate, it has become effective pursuant to Section 19(b)(3)(A)(iii) of the Act and subparagraph (f)(6) of Rule 19b-4 thereunder. At any time within 60 days of the filing of the proposed rule change, the Commission summarily may temporarily suspend such rule change if it appears to the Commission that such action is necessary or appropriate in the public interest, for the protection of investors, or otherwise in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. If the Commission takes such action, the Commission shall institute proceedings to determine whether the proposed rule should be approved or disapproved. IV. Solicitation of Comments Interested persons are invited to submit written data, views and arguments concerning the foregoing, including whether the proposed rule change is consistent with the Act. Comments may be submitted by any of the following methods: Electronic Comments Use the Commission's internet comment form (https://www.sec.gov/rules/sro.shtml); or Send an email to [email protected]. Please include file number SR-PHLX-2026-65 on the subject line. Paper Comments Send paper comments in triplicate to Secretary, Securities and Exchange Commission, 100 F Street NE, Washington, DC 20549-1090. All submissions should refer to file number SR-PHLX-2026-65. This file number should be included on the subject line if email is used. title: Self-Regulatory Organizations; New York Stock Exchange LLC; Notice of Filing and Immediate Effectiveness of Proposed Rule Change To Amend Rules 7.35 and 7.35A
raw_text:
Self-Regulatory Organizations; New York Stock Exchange LLC; Notice of Filing and Immediate Effectiveness of Proposed Rule Change To Amend Rules 7.35 and 7.35A

1. Purpose The Exchange proposes to amend Rule 7.35 (General) and Rule 7.35A (DMM-Facilitated Core Open and Trading Halt Auctions) to change when the Exchange begins disseminating Auction Imbalance Information for an IPO Auction. Specifically, the Exchange proposes to begin disseminating such information at the later of (A) 8:00 a.m. Eastern Time (``ET''), or (B) the earlier of (i) the time the Designated Market Maker (``DMM'') publishes the first pre-opening indication for the security pursuant to Rule 7.35A(d), or (ii) 10:00 a.m. ET. As discussed below, the Exchange currently begins disseminating Auction Imbalance Information for an IPO Auction at 8:00 a.m. ET, the same time applicable to all other Core Open Auctions, without regard to whether the underwriting syndicate has completed the IPO distribution process. This approach differs from that taken by at least one other national securities exchange, as described below. The Exchange believes that disseminating Auction Imbalance Information before the underwriting syndicate has finalized the distribution may result in information that does not reflect material aspects of the transaction and may therefore be misconstrued by market participants as indicative of the anticipated market for the security. The proposed change would better align the dissemination of Auction Imbalance Information with the liquidity formation process, thereby increasing transparency and reducing the potential for confusion, while preserving 8:00 a.m. ET as the earliest time such information may be disseminated, consistent with all other Core Open Auctions. Background Rule 7.35(c) governs the Exchange's dissemination of Auction Imbalance Information. Rule 7.35(c)(1) provides that Auction Imbalance Information is updated at least every second, unless there is no change to the information. Rule 7.35(c)(2) provides that Auction Imbalance Information is disseminated until the relevant Auction begins. Rule 7.35A(e) governs the timing, content, and pricing of Auction Imbalance Information specifically for the Core Open Auction and Trading Halt Auction facilitated by a DMM. Rule 7.35A(e)(1)(A) currently provides that, for the Core Open Auction, unless a security is halted, the Exchange will begin disseminating Auction Imbalance Information at 8:00 a.m. Rule 7.35A(e)(1)(D) further provides that the Exchange will not disseminate Auction Imbalance Information for the Core Open Auction if there is no ``Opening Reference Price,'' a term defined in Rule 7.35A(a). Rule 7.35A(e)(3) provides that the Imbalance Reference Price used in Auction Imbalance Information for the Core Open Auction is the Opening Reference Price, unless a pre-opening indication has been published, in which case it is the Opening Reference Price bounded by the pre-opening indication prices. Historically, Rule 7.35(c)(3) provided that the Exchange would not disseminate Auction Imbalance Information at all for a security that was an IPO or Direct Listing and had not yet had its IPO Auction or Direct Listing Auction. In April 2020, in connection with the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on the Exchange's Trading Floor operations, the Exchange adopted a series of temporary rule changes suspending this restriction so that Auction Imbalance Information would instead be disseminated for an IPO or Direct Listing in the same manner as for any other Core Open Auction. This temporary relief was subsequently extended on several occasions. In November 2020, the Exchange proposed to make this change permanent, which the Commission approved in 2021. As part of that filing, the Exchange deleted former Rule 7.35(c)(3) in its entirety such that an IPO or Direct Listing that had not yet had its IPO Auction or Direct Listing Auction would no longer be excluded from Auction Imbalance Information dissemination, and would instead be included in the same 8:00 a.m. dissemination applicable to Core Open Auctions generally. To enable the underlying calculation to function for a security with no trading history, the Exchange also amended the definition of the reference price used in that calculation to provide that, for an IPO that had not yet had its IPO Auction, the reference price would be deemed to be the security's offering price. The current definition of Opening Reference Price in Rule 7.35A(a) does not include an IPO-specific value. As described further below, the Exchange proposes to add such a value as part of this filing. Proposed Rule Change As noted, the Exchange's current practice of disseminating Auction Imbalance Information for an IPO Auction beginning at 8:00 a.m., i.e., at the same time as for any other Core Open Auction, differs from the approach taken by at least one other national securities exchange. Nasdaq, for example, does not begin disseminating its order imbalance indicator for an initial public offering until the beginning of the ``Display Only Period'' applicable to that security, and the subsequent ``Pre-Launch Period'' does not end until Nasdaq receives notice from the underwriter that the security is ready to trade. In addition, once disseminated, the reference price used in Nasdaq's imbalance indicator for an IPO is the price closest to the issuer's actual initial public offering price. As a result, Nasdaq's imbalance information for an IPO is not disseminated until information reflecting the completion of the underwriting syndicate's process is available. By contrast, because the Exchange currently begins disseminating Auction Imbalance Information for an IPO Auction at 8:00 a.m. ET, that information may be published before the underwriting syndicate has been finalized and before the DMM has issued a pre-opening indication reflecting the results of that process. At that stage, the information available to the Exchange, and therefore reflected in Auction Imbalance Information under the current approach, is limited. title: Self-Regulatory Organizations; MX2 LLC; Notice of Filing and Immediate Effectiveness of a Proposed Rule Change To Amend the Exchange's Fee Schedule
raw_text:
Self-Regulatory Organizations; MX2 LLC; Notice of Filing and Immediate Effectiveness of a Proposed Rule Change To Amend the Exchange's Fee Schedule

1. Purpose The purpose of the proposed rule change is to amend the Options Fee Schedule to (i) establish a separate category within the fee structure for fees and rebates on transactions in options overlying the Standard and Poor's Depositary Receipts Trust (``SPY''), the INVESCO QQQ Trust, Series 1 (``QQQ''), and the iShares Russell 2000 Index Fund (``IWM''), each of which are options in the Penny Interval Program (``Penny options''), (ii) reduce the Taker rebate for Customer transactions in SPY, QQQ and IWM options, and (iii) reduce the Maker fee for Market Maker transactions in SPY, QQQ and IWM options. Under the Options Fee Schedule, transactions are currently assessed a per contract fee (or provided a per contract rebate) dependent on the capacity of the Member, whether the underlying security is a Penny option or is not in the Penny Interval Program (Non-Penny option), and finally, whether the transaction adds (i.e., a ``Maker'') or removes (i.e., a ``Taker'') liquidity from the MX2 Options Book. Options on SPY, QQQ, and IWM are Penny options and are therefore currently subject to the rates applicable to Penny options. Specifically, for Penny options, including SPY, QQQ, and IWM, the Exchange currently provides a Customer Maker rebate of ($0.28) per contract and a Customer Taker rebate of ($0.48) per contract, and assesses a Maker fee of $0.50 per contract and a Taker fee of $0.50 per contract for Non-Customer transactions, including Market Maker, Professional, Firm, Away Market Maker, and Broker-Dealer transactions. The Exchange now proposes to establish separate fees and rebates for executions of options in SPY, QQQ and IWM, separately from other Penny options. To do so, the Exchange proposes to add a new column for SPY/QQQ/IWM to the transaction fee table in the Options Fee Schedule and to clarify in the heading of the existing Penny column that it applies to Penny options other than SPY/QQQ/IWM. The Exchange believes that separately accounting for SPY, QQQ, and IWM is appropriate because these options are highly liquid and are commonly treated separately by other options exchanges. As noted above, as it relates to Professional, Firm, Away Market Maker, and Broker-Dealer executions of SPY, QQQ, and IWM options, the Exchange is not proposing to change the fees currently assessed, it is simply carving out SPY, QQQ and IWM into a separate category within the fee structure. Said another way, the proposed SPY, QQQ and IWM fees for Professional, Firm, Away Market Maker, and Broker-Dealer transactions will continue to be the same fees assessed to transactions in Penny options currently. As it relates to Customer transactions, the Exchange is proposing to provide the same Maker rebate for SPY, QQQ and IWM as the rebate applicable to Penny options currently, but to reduce the applicable Taker rebate. As it relates to Market Maker transactions, the Exchange is proposing to assess the same Taker fee for SPY, QQQ and IWM as the fee applicable to Penny options currently, but to reduce the applicable Maker fee. The Exchange notes that it operates in a highly competitive market in which market participants can readily direct order flow to competing venues if they deem fee levels at a particular venue to be excessive or incentives to be insufficient. The Exchange is one of only 20 options venues to which market participants may direct their order flow. Based on publicly available information, no single options exchange has more than approximately 18.1% of the market share and currently the Exchange represents only approximately 0.4% of the market share. In such a low-concentrated and highly competitive market, no single options exchange, including the Exchange, possesses significant pricing power in the execution of option order flow. The Exchange believes that the ever-shifting market share among the exchanges from month to month demonstrates that market participants can shift order flow, discontinue, or reduce use of certain categories of products in response to fee changes. Accordingly competitive forces constrain the Exchange's transaction fees, and market participants can readily trade on competing venues if they deem pricing levels at those other venues to be more favorable. The Exchange's Fee Schedule sets forth standard rebates and rates applied per contract. Under the new category of transactions fees and rebates assessed for SPY, QQQ, and IWM options, the Exchange is proposing the following: For Customer transactions, the Exchange is proposing to provide a rebate of ($0.28) per contract for executions that add liquidity and a rebate of ($0.21) per contract for executions that remove liquidity in SPY, QQQ, and IWM options. Accordingly, the Exchange notes that Customers will receive the same Maker rebate for all Penny options, including SPY, QQQ and IWM, however, the Exchange is proposing to reduce the Taker rebate for executions of SPY, QQQ and IWM options from ($0.48) per contract to ($0.21) per contract. For SPY, QQQ, and IWM Market Maker transactions, the Exchange is proposing to assess a fee of $0.20 per contract for executions that add liquidity and a fee of $0.50 per contract for executions that remove liquidity. Accordingly, the Exchange notes that Market Makers will be assessed the same Taker fee for all Penny options, including SPY, QQQ and IWM, however, the Market Maker Maker fee for executions of SPY, QQQ and IWM options is lower than that assessed for executions of all other Penny options, which will continue to be $0.50 per contract. Lastly, as noted above, for all other transactions (i.e., Professional, Firm, Away Market Maker, and Broker-Dealer), the Exchange is proposing to assess a fee of $0.50 per contract for executions that add liquidity in SPY, QQQ and IWM options, and a fee of $0.50 per contract for executions that remove liquidity in SPY, QQQ, and IWM Options. title: Self-Regulatory Organizations; Investors Exchange LLC; Notice of Filing and Immediate Effectiveness of Proposed Rule Change To Extend the Implementation Timeframe of a Recent Rule Filing
raw_text:
Self-Regulatory Organizations; Investors Exchange LLC; Notice of Filing and Immediate Effectiveness of Proposed Rule Change To Extend the Implementation Timeframe of a Recent Rule Filing

1. Purpose IEX is filing this proposal to extend the implementation timeframe of the rule changes proposed in SR-IEX-2026-19 to provide that certain pegged order types and the D-Limit order type will be eligible for trading during the Exchange's Pre-Market Session and Post-Market Session. Pursuant to the Original Rule Filing, the Exchange will announce the implementation date of the proposed rule change by Trading Alert at least ten days in advance of such implementation date and within 90 days of effectiveness of the proposed rule change. The Original Rule Filing was immediately effective on the date of filing, July 10, 2026, which meant the Trading Alert would issue no later than 90 days later, i.e., on October 8, 2026. On September 2, 2026, the Exchange filed to extend the implementation timeframe of the rule changes to December 7, 2026. In order to complete all steps in IEX's standard deployment schedule, IEX has determined that it requires more time than provided for by the Original Rule Filing and Initial Extension to determine the implementation date and issue a Trading Alert announcing such date. Thus, IEX now proposes extending the December 7, 2026 Trading Alert deadline to the end of the first quarter of 2027. As proposed, on or before the end of the first quarter of 2027, IEX will still announce the implementation date by Trading Alert at least ten days in advance of such implementation date. Besides this change, the Exchange is not proposing to make any changes to the terms of the Original Rule Filing. 2. Rather, postponing implementation will allow the Exchange to implement the original rule change in a thorough and risk averse manner and is not designed for any competitive purpose. C. The Exchange has asked that the Commission waive the 30-day operative delay so that the proposed rule change may become operative immediately upon filing. The Exchange states that waiver of the operative delay would permit the Exchange to implement this proposal on or prior to December 7, 2026, the date by which the Original Rule Filing, as extended by the Initial Extension, requires the Exchange to issue a Trading Alert, thereby avoiding any potential confusion on the part of market participants or the Commission as to when the original proposed rule change will be implemented. 1. Purpose The Exchange proposes to eliminate the requirement that the Exchange distribute an information circular to Members prior to the commencement of trading in each UTP Exchange Traded Product that generally includes the same information as contained in the information circular provided by the listing exchange as provided in 24X Rule 14.1(b)(1). The Exchange also proposes to amend 24X Rule 14.1(a) to add express cross-references to 24X Rules 3.7 and 3.21. The Exchange also proposes to amend 24X Rule 14.1(b)(2)(B) to require that the written description referenced therein be provided in a form approved by the listing exchange or prepared by the open-ended management company issuing such securities. Finally, the Exchange proposes to renumber 24X Rules 14.1(b)(2) through (5) as 24X Rules 14.1(b)(1) through (4), respectively. 24X Rule 14.1(b) governs the trading of UTP Exchange Traded Products, which are securities listed on another national securities exchange that trade on the Exchange pursuant to unlisted trading privileges (``UTP''). Under current 24X Rule 14.1(b)(1), the Exchange must distribute an information circular prior to the commencement of trading in each UTP Exchange Traded Product that generally mirrors the information circular issued by the primary listing exchange, including: (a) the special risks of trading the new Exchange Traded Product; (b) the Exchange Rules that will apply to the new Exchange Traded Product; and (c) information about the dissemination of the value of the underlying assets or indices. The Exchange proposes to delete 24X Rule 14.1(b)(1) in its entirety. The information circular requirement is unnecessary because the primary listing exchange's information circular already provides Members with the same disclosures the Exchange would otherwise be required to produce. Members have access to the primary listing exchange's information circular prior to the commencement of UTP trading and may rely upon it for the same purposes. The Exchange's issuance of a separate, duplicative circular therefore serves no independent investor protection function. The Exchange also proposes to amend 24X Rule 14.1(a) to add express cross-references to 24X Rule 3.7 (Recommendations to Customers) and 24X Rule 3.21 (Customer Disclosures). The Exchange is adding express cross- references to those rules in the introductory paragraph of 24X Rule 14.1(a) to enhance their visibility in the context of UTP Exchange Traded Products. These rules already apply to Members by operation of the Exchange's rulebook. The cross-references are intended to make the applicable framework explicit in the context of UTP Exchange Traded Products. 24X Rule 3.7 independently requires Members to ensure that any recommendation of a UTP Exchange Traded Product is suitable for the customer based on the customer's investment profile, a standing obligation that applies regardless of whether the Exchange has issued a product-specific information circular. Similarly, 24X Rule 3.21 independently requires Members to provide customers with a written disclosure of the risks of trading outside of Regular Trading Hours before accepting any order for execution during such sessions, a standing obligation not contingent on the Exchange's issuance of a product-specific information circular. Because 24X Rule 14.1(b)(1) has historically served as the mechanism through which the Exchange satisfies the notification obligation under 24X Rule 14.1(b)(2)(B), deletion of 24X Rule 14.1(b)(1) necessitates a conforming amendment to 24X Rule 14.1(b)(2)(B). The Exchange proposes to amend 24X Rule 14.1(b)(2)(B) to require that the written description referenced therein be provided in a form approved by the listing exchange or prepared by the open-ended management company issuing such securities. The Exchange will notify Members by information circular that such written description will only be required when mandated by the listing exchange. This amendment is consistent with the broader purpose of the proposed rule change: where the listing exchange's information circular already provides Members with the information necessary to assess a UTP Exchange Traded Product, a duplicative written description obligation serves no independent investor protection function. Members may rely on the listing exchange's information circular in the same manner and to the same effect. Finally, the Exchange proposes to renumber existing 24X Rules 14.1(b)(2) through (5) as 24X Rules 14.1(b)(1) through (4), respectively. 2. Self-Regulatory Organizations; Financial Industry Regulatory Authority, Inc.; Notice of Filing of a Proposed Rule Change To Amend the FINRA By-Laws, the FINRA Regulation By-Laws, the Plan of Allocation and Delegation of Functions by FINRA to Subsidiaries, FINRA's Restated Certificate of Incorporation, and FINRA Rule 5110

1. Purpose Background The FINRA By-Laws, read together with the Certificate of Incorporation, govern the composition and operation of the FINRA Board. The Board includes individuals from member firms of various sizes and business models, as well as public leaders with expertise in markets, technology, regulatory oversight, business and law. In 1996, FINRA's predecessor, the National Association of Securities Dealers (``NASD''), amended its By-Laws to require that the number of non-industry Governors exceed the number of industry Governors. The majority public structure was implemented when the By-Laws were last amended in 2007 in connection with the merger of NASD and NYSE Regulation to create FINRA. The FINRA By-Laws currently provide for a Board composed of up to 25 Governors, with 10 seats designated for ``Industry Governors,'' 11 to 14 seats designated for ``Public Governors'' and one seat reserved for FINRA's Chief Executive Officer (``CEO''), who is considered neither an Industry Governor nor a Public Governor. Seven of the Industry Governor seats--three Small Firm Governors, one Mid-Size Firm Governor and three Large Firm Governors--are designated for individuals associated with FINRA members that correspond to each firm size. Pursuant to the FINRA By-Laws, a small firm employs at least one and no more than 150 registered persons; a mid-size firm employs at least 151 and no more than 499 registered persons; and a large firm employs 500 or more registered persons. (See FINRA By-Laws Article I.) Industry Governors are elected to these seats by the small, mid-size and large member firms, respectively. The three remaining Industry Governor seats are appointed, segment-specific seats, i.e., a ``Floor Member Governor,'' an ``Independent Dealer/ Insurance Affiliate Governor'' and an ``Investment Company Affiliate Governor,'' as those terms are defined in the FINRA By-Laws. (See FINRA By-Laws Article I.) Overview of Proposed Amendments FINRA is proposing to amend the FINRA By-Laws, FINRA Regulation By- Laws and Delegation Plan relating to the composition and operation of the FINRA Board and Board committees to modernize FINRA's governance structure and strengthen FINRA's self-regulatory model. As described below, FINRA is further proposing to amend the Certificate of Incorporation to conform relevant provisions to the amended and restated FINRA By-Laws and to make other updates and technical changes. Among other changes, the proposed rule change would transition the FINRA Board from a majority of Public Governors to a majority of Industry Governors, while preserving a substantial role for public representatives on the Board--Public Governors would represent from 41.7 to 47.4 percent of the total number of Industry and Public Governors. The proposed rule change also would potentially broaden industry representation, including among small firms, on the FINRA Board by converting the three appointed, segment-specific industry seats to three appointed, at-large industry seats. And, consistent with modern governance practices, the proposed rule change would reduce the size of the Board, which currently may have up to 25 members, to no more than 20 members. With respect to the operation of the FINRA Board and Board committees, the proposed rule change would revise term limits, conform quorum requirements and provide more flexibility for the Board to manage the composition of the Board and its committees based on current needs, subject to minimum Industry and Public Governor representation requirements. The Audit Committee would continue to require a majority of Public Governors and continue to be chaired by a Public Governor, as is the case today. FINRA believes that the proposed rule change would strengthen member engagement, increase access to industry expertise and better position FINRA to protect and serve investors, markets and member firms in an evolving industry and market environment. FINRA believes that the public benefits of the self-regulatory organization (``SRO'') model include the ability to leverage member knowledge, experience and insight. Appropriate member participation in FINRA's programs is important for capturing the deep, practical expertise that is central to self-regulation and helps FINRA effectively carry out its mission of protecting investors and market integrity-- including by producing better visibility into emerging threats, risky business practices and unfair tactics. In addition, the proposed rule change would provide the Board greater flexibility to draw on expertise from a broader range of business models to adapt to changes in the industry and ensure appropriate representation from across the membership--enhancing opportunities for a wider spectrum of member firms, including more small firms, to participate in governance. Finally, with a somewhat smaller size and greater flexibility to manage its operations, the Board would be more nimble and better able to benefit from the insights of both Industry and Public Governors. FINRA notes that several of the factors that supported NASD's adoption of a majority non-industry Board over 30 years ago are significantly different from the environment FINRA faces today. NASD's change to its Board composition was one of many changes made in connection with an SEC enforcement action against NASD, which found that NASD failed to adequately oversee the Nasdaq market and that Nasdaq market makers exercised undue influence over NASD's operations and regulatory affairs. NASD fully divested Nasdaq in 2006, eliminating the market-driven conflicts of interest that had previously existed between NASD's self- regulatory obligations and the competitive incentives of Nasdaq market makers. 1. Purpose The Exchange proposes to amend 24X Rule 11.14 (``Clearly Erroneous Executions'') in light of the Commission's approval of Overnight Protected Bands under the LULD Plan for 23/5 Trading. Background In conjunction with the industry's plans for the introduction of trading 23 hours a day, 5 days a week (``23/5 Trading''), the Operating Committee of the Plan to Address Extraordinary Market Volatility (``LULD Plan'') filed proposed Amendment 27 to the LULD Plan, which proposed to establish price band protections during overnight trading hours (``Overnight Price Bands''). The Operating Committee proposed that the Overnight Price Bands would initially be temporary static bands 20% above and below two reference points, and that after implementation, the Operating Committee would evaluate the performance of such Overnight Price Bands and propose appropriate changes in a new plan amendment. On August 5, 2026, the Commission approved the proposal. In light of the Commission's approval of these changes to the LULD Plan, the Exchange now proposes several amendments to 24X Rule 11.14 regarding Clearly Erroneous Executions. In general, the rule describes the process a market participant may use to request cancellation of a transaction that was ``clearly erroneous.'' The current rule's central premise is that if LULD Price Bands under the LULD Plan were available and correct at the time the transaction was executed, the transaction is not eligible for clearly erroneous review. Specifically, 24X Rule 11.14(c)(1) currently provides that ``[i]f the execution time of the transaction(s) under review is during Regular Trading Hours, the transaction will not be reviewable as clearly erroneous'' except in certain limited circumstances, including when (A) the transaction is in an NMS stock that is not subject to the LULD Plan (e.g., rights and warrants), (B) the transaction was executed at a time when LULD Price Bands were unavailable or trading should have been prevented due to a regulatory halt or other halt, or (C) several other limited circumstances. In approving the existing version of the rule, the Commission noted that restricting clearly erroneous review in this way during times when LULD Price Bands were in effect was ``consistent with the Act and will further the goal of providing greater certainty to market participants that trades executed within the Price Bands will stand and not be broken. . . . Thus, the proposal is designed to limit the potential discordance between the LULD mechanism and CEE review process.'' Currently, LULD Price Bands are available only during Regular Trading Hours, meaning that the restrictions on clearly erroneous review described above apply only during Regular Trading Hours. With the introduction of Overnight Price Bands, the Exchange now proposes to extend the existing restrictions on clearly erroneous review to the period when Overnight Price Bands are in place. This proposed change would be consistent with the Commission's rationale in approving the current version of the rule because it would limit any potential discordance between the LULD mechanism and CEE review in the overnight trading session, providing greater certainty to market participants that trades executed with the Overnight Price Bands will stand and not be broken. 24X Rule 11.14 currently provides that transactions executed during the 24X Market Session are treated in the same manner as transactions executed during the Pre-Market and Post-Market Sessions. Given the Commission's approval of Overnight Price Bands, the Exchange proposes instead to make clearly erroneous review of transactions executed during the 24X Market Session available in a manner similar to transactions executed during Regular Trading Hours. Proposed Changes to 24X Rule 11.14(c)(1) To implement this change, the Exchange proposes to add several definitions to 24X Rule 11.14(c)(1). First, the Exchange would add that the term ``LULD Protected Hours'' includes Regular Trading Hours and ``Overnight Protected Hours'' defined in Section VIII of the LULD Plan. Second, the Exchange would define ``LULD Price Bands'' or ``Price Bands'' to mean the Price Bands defined in Section V of the LULD Plan (i.e., the Price Bands that apply during Regular Trading Hours) and ``Overnight Price Bands'' as defined in Section VIII of the LULD Plan (i.e., the Price Bands that apply to the Overnight Protected Hours from 9:00 p.m. ET through 4:00 a.m. ET). The Exchange proposes to amend the current first sentence of 24X Rule 11.14(c)(1) to replace the phrase ``Regular Trading Hours'' with ``LULD Protected Hours,'' to provide that ``[i]f the execution time of the transaction(s) under review is during LULD Protected Hours, the transaction will not be reviewable as clearly erroneous . . . .'' This change would extend the LULD-based restrictions on clearly erroneous review currently in place during Regular Trading Hours to the Overnight Protected Hours. The Exchange also proposes to amend 24X Rule 11.14(c)(1)(B)'s reference to ``Percentage Parameter'' to incorporate the Percentage Parameter that applies to Overnight Protected Hours. 1. Purpose Trades in listed securities occasionally occur at prices that deviate from prevailing market prices, and those trades sometimes establish a high, low or last sale price for a security that does not reflect its true market. The Consolidated Tape Association (``CTA'') Plan and the Nasdaq UTP Plan (``UTP Plan'') each offer participants in such plans with the discretion to append an Aberrant Report Indicator to a trade report to indicate that the market believes that the trade price of a particular trade executed on the participant's market does not accurately reflect the prevailing market for the security in question. Several national securities exchanges, including The New York Stock Exchange (``NYSE'') and Nasdaq Stock Market (``Nasdaq''), and more recently, Investors Exchange LLC (``IEX'') and NYSE Texas, Inc. (``NYSE Texas''), have adopted policies related to use of the Aberrant Report Indicator for equities trades that, while not eligible for cancellation pursuant to applicable exchange rules governing clearly erroneous executions, are determined not to accurately reflect the prevailing market for the security in question. The Exchange believes that such policies are appropriate to identify such trades to vendors and market participants so that they may exclude such trades from relevant pricing metrics (e.g., high, low and last sale prices). Accordingly, TXSE is proposing to adopt a policy substantially similar to the existing policies of such other national securities exchanges as described below. During the course of surveillance by the Exchange or as a result of notification by another market, listed company, or market participant, the Exchange may become aware of trade prices that do not accurately reflect the prevailing market for a particular security. In such a case, the Exchange will contact the listing exchange (if the Exchange is not the listing exchange) and other markets (in the case of executions that take place across multiple markets) to seek consensus as to whether the trade price is consistent with the prevailing market for the security. If the Exchange determines that the trade price is inconsistent with the prevailing market for the security after considering the factors discussed below, the Exchange will append an Aberrant Report Indicator to the trade pursuant to applicable CTA and UTP procedures. Appending an Aberrant Report Indicator to the trade will have no effect on the validity of the underlying trade. The proposed policy would be applicable to trades that occur on TXSE, whether traded on an unlisted trading privilege (``UTP'') basis or listed on TXSE. In making the determination to append the Aberrant Report Indicator to a particular trade, the Exchange shall consider all factors related to a trade, including, but not limited to, the following: Material news released for the security; Suspicious trading activity; System malfunctions or disruptions; Locked or crossed markets; A recent trading halt or resumption of trading in the security; Whether the security is in its initial public offering; Volume and volatility for the security; Whether the trade represents a 52-week high or low for the security; Whether the trade price deviates significantly from recent trading patterns in the security; Whether the trade price reflects a stock-split, reorganization or other corporate action; The validity of consolidated tape trades and quotes in comparison to national best bids and offers; and The general volatility of market conditions. In determining whether trade prices are inconsistent with the prevailing market, the Exchange proposes that its policy shall be to follow the following general guidelines: The Exchange will review whether a trade price does not reflect the prevailing market for a security if the trade occurs during regular trading hours (i.e., 9:30 a.m. to 4 p.m.) and occurs at a price that deviates from the ``Reference Price'' by an amount that meets or exceeds the following thresholds: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ Numerical Trade price threshold (percent) ------------------------------------------------------------------------ Between $0 and $15.00....................................... 7 Between $15.01 and $50.00................................... 5 In excess of $50.00......................................... 3 ------------------------------------------------------------------------ The ``Reference Price'' refers to (a) if the primary market for the security is open at the time of the trade, the national best bid or offer for the security, or (b) if the primary market for the security is not open at the time of the trade, the first executable quote or print for the security on the primary market after execution of the trade in question. However, if the circumstances suggest that a different Reference Price would be more appropriate, the Exchange will use the different Reference Price. For instance, if the national best bid and offer for the security are so wide apart as to fail to reflect the market for the security, the Exchange might use as the Reference Price a trade price or best bid or offer that was available prior to the trade in question. If TXSE determines that a trade price does not reflect the prevailing market for a security and the trade represented the last sale of the security on the Exchange during a trading session, the Exchange may also determine to remove that trade's designation as the last sale and the preceding last sale eligible trade would become the new last sale. Purpose The Exchange proposes to amend Section 115(f)(3) of Equity 7 (Pricing Schedule) to provide that the Dedicated OUCH Port Infrastructure subscription service offered under that provision is available to support Day Session ports only and is not available to support Night Session ports. The Dedicated OUCH Port Infrastructure service allows a member firm to assign up to 30 of its OUCH ports to a dedicated server infrastructure for its exclusive use. An OUCH port is a connectivity port designated to accept only OUCH protocol messaging, which provides a method for subscribers to send orders and receive status updates on those orders. A Dedicated OUCH Port Infrastructure subscription is available to a member firm for a fee of $5,000 per month, which is in addition to the standard fees assessed for each OUCH port. A one-time installation fee of $5,000 is assessed to subscribers for each Dedicated OUCH Port Infrastructure subscription. The service is optional and is available to all member firms. Absent a subscription, the Exchange distributes a member firm's OUCH ports among shared servers, which act as switches that channel the message traffic a member firm sends through its ports to the Exchange's system. All port servers, including the servers used for the Dedicated OUCH Port Infrastructure service, are owned and operated by the Exchange, and a subscribing member firm does not have physical access to its dedicated server or the ability to modify it. The Exchange now proposes to amend Section 115(f)(3) of Equity 7 to provide that the Dedicated OUCH Port Infrastructure subscription service is available to support Day Session ports only and is not available to support Night Session ports. The reason for the proposed change is that the Exchange has determined that separating the operation of Day Session ports and Night Session ports, as proposed, is appropriate to facilitate the orderly maintenance and operation of its ports generally. The Exchange therefore proposes to state expressly in its rules that the Dedicated OUCH Port Infrastructure service supports Day Session ports only, and that the offering is not available to support Night Session ports. The Exchange anticipates that fewer than ten subscribers will be affected by the proposed rule change. To continue using their Night Session ports, each affected subscriber need only place its Night Session ports on shared server infrastructure at no additional cost, as Exchange customers that do not subscribe to the Dedicated OUCH Port Infrastructure subscription service do today. Night Session OUCH ports placed on shared servers will remain subject to the fees otherwise applicable to OUCH ports under Section 115 of Equity 7. The Dedicated OUCH Port Infrastructure subscription service, including its fees, will continue to be available to support Day Session ports without change. The Exchange believes that the proposed rule change is reasonable. The Dedicated OUCH Port Infrastructure subscription service is optional, and a subscriber will continue to receive the same service for the same subscription fee in support of its Day Session ports. The Exchange has determined that separating the operation of Day Session and Night Session ports is appropriate to facilitate the orderly maintenance and operation of its ports generally. Thus, the Exchange proposes to specify that the Dedicated OUCH Port Infrastructure subscription service is available for Day Session ports only and that the service is not available to support the use of Night Session ports. The Exchange notes that Night Session ports remain subject to the fees otherwise applicable to OUCH ports under Section 115 of Equity 7. The Exchange believes that the proposed rule change is an equitable allocation of fees and is not unfairly discriminatory. The proposal applies uniformly to all member firms and turns on the trading session the optional connectivity offering supports, not on the identity of the member firm. Every member firm will connect its Night Session ports in the same manner, whether or not it subscribes to the service for its Day Session ports. The Exchange also believes that the proposed rule change promotes just and equitable principles of trade and removes impediments to and perfects the mechanism of a free and open market and a national market system by stating clearly in its rules which ports the service supports, so that member firms can arrange their Night Session connectivity accordingly. title: Self-Regulatory Organizations; MEMX LLC; Notice of Filing and Immediate Effectiveness of a Proposed Rule Change To Amend the Exchange's Fee Schedule
raw_text:
Self-Regulatory Organizations; MEMX LLC; Notice of Filing and Immediate Effectiveness of a Proposed Rule Change To Amend the Exchange's Fee Schedule

1. Purpose The purpose of the proposed rule change is to amend the Fee Schedule to: (i) adopt a new DLI Tier 1 and re-designate the existing DLI Tiers 1 and 2 as DLI Tiers 2 and 3, respectively; and (ii) provide that the additive rebates under the Tape A Quoting Tier, Tape B Volume Tier 1, Tape B Volume Tier 2, and Tape C Quoting Tier are not eligible to be combined with any DLI Tier rebate, each as further described below. The Exchange first notes that it operates in a highly competitive market in which market participants can readily direct order flow to competing venues if they deem fee levels at a particular venue to be excessive or incentives to be insufficient. More specifically, the Exchange is only one of 18 registered equities exchanges, as well as a number of alternative trading systems and other off-exchange venues, to which market participants may direct their order flow. Based on publicly available information, no single registered equities exchange currently has more than approximately 14% of the total market share of executed volume of equities trading. Thus, in such a low- concentrated and highly competitive market, no single equities exchange possesses significant pricing power in the execution of order flow, and the Exchange currently represents approximately 1.6% of the overall market share. The Exchange in particular operates a ``Maker-Taker'' model whereby it provides rebates to Members that add liquidity to the Exchange and charges fees to Members that remove liquidity from the Exchange. The Fee Schedule sets forth the standard rebates and fees applied per share for orders that add and remove liquidity, respectively. Additionally, in response to the competitive environment, the Exchange also offers tiered pricing, which provides Members with opportunities to qualify for higher rebates or lower fees where certain volume criteria and thresholds are met. Tiered pricing provides an incremental incentive for Members to strive for higher tier levels, which provides increasingly higher benefits or discounts for satisfying increasingly more stringent criteria. Currently, the Exchange provides a standard rebate of $0.0015 per share for executions of orders in securities priced at or above $1.00 per share that add displayed liquidity to the Exchange (such orders, ``Added Displayed Volume''). The Exchange also offers enhanced rebates for executions of Added Displayed Volume under the Displayed Liquidity Incentive (``DLI'') Tiers, as well as additive rebates for qualifying executions of Added Displayed Volume in Tape A, Tape B and Tape C securities, each as described below. Adoption of New DLI Tier 1 and Re-Designation of Existing DLI Tiers The Exchange currently offers DLI Tiers 1 and 2 under which a Member may receive an enhanced rebate for executions of Added Displayed Volume by achieving the corresponding required criteria for each such tier. The DLI Tiers are designed to encourage Members, through the provision of an enhanced rebate for executions of Added Displayed Volume, to promote price discovery and market quality by quoting at the NBBO for a significant portion of each day (i.e., through the applicable quoting requirement ) in a broad base of securities (i.e., through the applicable securities requirement ), thereby benefitting the Exchange and investors by providing improved trading conditions for all market participants through narrower bid-ask spreads and increased depth of liquidity available at the NBBO in a broad base of securities and committing capital to support the execution of orders. Currently, under DLI Tier 1, the Exchange provides an enhanced rebate of $0.0032 per share for executions of Added Displayed Volume for Members that qualify for such tier by achieving an NBBO Time of at least 50% in an average of at least 1,000 securities per trading day during the month. Under DLI Tier 2, the Exchange currently provides an enhanced rebate of $0.0026 per share for executions of Added Displayed Volume for Members that qualify for such tier by achieving an NBBO Time of at least 25% in an average of at least 500 securities per trading day during the month. The Exchange now proposes to adopt a new DLI Tier 1 under which the Exchange would provide an enhanced rebate of $0.0035 per share for executions of Added Displayed Volume for Members that qualify for such tier by achieving an NBBO Time of at least 50% in an average of at least 1,300 securities per trading day during the month. In connection with the adoption of the proposed new DLI Tier 1, the Exchange proposes to re-designate the existing DLI Tier 1 as DLI Tier 2 and the existing DLI Tier 2 as DLI Tier 3. The rebates and the required criteria under the re-designated DLI Tiers 2 and 3 are not changing, and the pricing under such tiers would continue to be available to Members on the same terms as it is today. In addition, the Exchange is not proposing to change the rebate provided under any DLI Tier for executions of orders in securities priced below $1.00 per share, which would continue to be 0.15% of the total dollar value of the transaction. The proposed new DLI Tier 1 is designed to reward Members that quote at the NBBO for a significant portion of each day in a broader set of securities than is currently required under any DLI Tier. Specifically, the securities requirement under the proposed new DLI Tier 1 (1,300 securities) is 300 securities greater than the securities requirement under the existing DLI Tier 1 (which would become DLI Tier 2), while the quoting requirement (50%) is the same. In exchange for meeting these more stringent criteria, the Exchange proposes to provide a rebate that is $0.0003 per share higher than the rebate provided under the existing DLI Tier 1. 1. Purpose The Exchange proposes to amend its listing rules at ISE Options 4, Section 3, Criteria for Underlying Securities. Specifically, the Exchange proposes to amend the criteria for listing options on Exchange-Traded Fund Shares (``ETFs'') at Options 4, Section 3(h). Background Currently, Options 4, Section 3(h)(vi) specifies that ISE may list and trade options on shares or other securities that represent interests in a Commodity-Based Trust that meet the generic criteria of Nasdaq Rule 5711(d) provided the Trust holds a single crypto asset or multiple crypto assets. Further, a Commodity-Based Trust that meets the requirements of Options 4, Section 3(h)(vi) must also satisfy the following requirements: (A) the total global supply of each underlying crypto asset(s) held by the Commodity-Based Trust has an average daily market value of at least $700 million over the last 12 months; and (B) each crypto asset held by the Commodity-Based Trust underlies a derivatives contract that trades on a market with which the Exchange has a comprehensive surveillance sharing agreement, whether directly or through common membership in the Intermarket Surveillance Group (``ISG''). Proposal In light of the recent approval of a rule change by Nasdaq (``SR- NASDAQ-2026-032'' or ``CBT Proposal'') that modified the generic listing standards for Commodity-Based Trust Shares at Nasdaq Rule 5711(d), the Exchange proposes to amend Options 4, Section 3(h)(3) to align this options rule with the rule text adopted in SR-NASDAQ-2026- 032, which will permit the Exchange to list options on Commodity-Based Trust Shares that meet the revised listing standards of Nasdaq Rule 5711(d). Digital Commodity vs. Crypto Asset First, the Exchange proposes to amend Options 4, Section 3(h) to replace the term ``crypto asset'' with the term ``digital commodity.'' The term ``crypto asset'' is defined at Options 4, Section 3(h) to mean an asset that is generated, issued and/or transferred using a blockchain or similar distributive ledger technology network, including, but not limited to, assets known as ``tokens,'' ``digital assets,'' ``virtual currencies,'' and ``coins'' and that relies on cryptographic protocols. The term ``digital commodity'' is defined at Nasdaq Rule 5711(d)(iii)(D) to mean a commodity that is a digital asset and is intrinsically linked to and derives its value from the programmatic operation of a functional crypto system, as well as supply and demand dynamics, rather than from the expectation of profits from the essential managerial efforts of others. This proposal is intended to align the options terminology with the terminology utilized in Nasdaq Rule 5711(d), which is the basis for listing options on Commodity-Based Trust Shares. The proposed definition of ``digital commodity'' is informed by the joint interpretative guidance issued by the SEC and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (``CFTC''), effective March 23, 2026. The Exchange represents that to the extent legislation is enacted defining ``digital commodity'' or a substantially similar term, the Exchange will submit a rule filing to conform the definition in Options 4, Section 3(h) to the statutory definition. As defined, the term ``crypto asset'' captures anything that (1) is generated, issued, or transferred on a blockchain or similar Distributed Ledger Technology (``DLT'') network and (2) relies on cryptographic protocols. It is technology-defined and deliberately inclusive (``including but not limited to'' tokens, virtual currencies, coins, etc.). There is no mention of economic function, value source, or regulatory character. In contrast, the term ``digital commodity,'' as proposed, is a narrower classification that sits inside the broader crypto-asset universe. Not every crypto asset qualifies as a digital commodity. The Exchange believes that aligning the terminology associated with the generic listing standards for options on Commodity-Based Trust Shares at Options 4, Section 3(h)(vi) with the generic listing standards for Commodity-Based Trust Shares in Nasdaq Rule 5711(d) will allow the Exchange to list options on Commodity-Based Trust Shares that Nasdaq may list pursuant to Nasdaq Rule 5711(d) as amended by the CBT Proposal. Comprehensive Surveillance Sharing Agreement Second, to more closely align the listing of options on Commodity- Based Trust Shares pursuant to Options 4, Section 3(h)(vi) with the listing of Commodity-Based Trust Shares that may be listed pursuant to Nasdaq Rule 5711(d), the Exchange proposes to amend Options 4, Section 3(h)(3)(B) to require that each digital commodity held by the Commodity-Based Trust underlie a derivatives contract that trades on a market with which the Exchange has a comprehensive surveillance sharing agreement, whether directly or through common membership in the ISG, except that up to 15% of the net asset value (``NAV'') of the Commodity-Based Trust's holdings in the aggregate may consist of digital commodities that do not meet this requirement. 1. Purpose The Exchange proposes to increase the NDX options fees for regular orders assessed to Non-Priority Customer market participants in Options 7, Section 3. As set forth in Options 7, Section 3, the Exchange currently assesses a fee of $0.75 per contract for NDX Market Maker, Non- Nasdaq GEMX Market Maker (FarMM), Firm Proprietary /Broker-Dealer and Professional Customer regular orders. Priority Customer orders are currently assessed a $0.50 per contract fee in NDX. The Exchange now proposes to increase the Non-Priority Customer NDX fees for regular orders from $0.75 to $1.25 per contract. As a result, Non-Priority Customer orders would each be assessed a fee of $1.25 per contract in NDX. The Exchange is not proposing to amend the Priority Customer fee of $0.50 per contract in NDX, or the fees for other index options in Options 7, Section 3. The notes to Options 7, Section 3 would continue to apply, unchanged. Specifically: (i) note 6 provides that the index options fees apply only to NDX; the fees are assessed to all executions in NDX; (ii) note 9 provides that for transactions in NDX, a license surcharge of $0.25 is assessed to Non-Priority Customers; (iii) note 14 provides that a surcharge of $0.25 per contract is assessed to all market participants for executions in NDX with a premium price of $25.00 or greater; and (iv) note 20 provides that a surcharge is assessed to electronic simple Non-Priority Customer orders in NDX that remove liquidity according to a premium schedule, which ranges from $1.00 per contract for premiums of less than $3.00 to $3.00 per contract for premiums greater than or equal to $50.00. By way of example, under the proposed pricing a Market Maker electronic simple order in NDX with a premium of $5.00 that adds liquidity would be assessed $1.50 per contract ($1.25 fee plus the $0.25 per contract surcharge in note 9), as compared to $1.00 per contract today ($0.75 fee plus the $0.25 per contract surcharge in note 9). If the same order removed liquidity, it would be assessed $3.00 per contract (the $1.25 fee, the $0.25 per contract surcharge in note 9, plus the $1.50 note 20 surcharge), as compared to $2.50 per contract today (the $0.75 fee, the $0.25 per contract surcharge in note 9, plus the $1.50 note 20 surcharge). A Professional Customer simple order in NDX with a premium of $30.00 that adds liquidity would be assessed $1.75 per contract (the $1.25 fee plus the $0.25 surcharge in note 9 plus the $0.25 note 14 surcharge) as compared to $1.25 per contract today (the $0.75 fee plus the $0.25 surcharge plus the $0.25 note 14 surcharge). By comparison, a Priority Customer simple order in NDX that adds liquidity with a premium of $30.00 would continue to be assessed $0.75 per contract (the $0.50 fee plus the $0.25 note 14 surcharge. While the Exchange is increasing the NDX Non-Priority Customer fee, the Exchange believes that market participants will continue to transact NDX options on GEMX given the large notional value of NDX. Each options contract has a multiplier of $100, so a single contract represents notional exposure equal to $100 times the index level. For example, at an index level of 20,000, one NDX contract represents approximately $2,000,000 in notional value. At that level, the proposed $1.25 per contract fee represents approximately 0.00625 basis points of notional value, and the proposed $0.50 increase represents approximately 0.0025 basis points. Because the Exchange's fees are assessed per contract regardless of the size of the underlying exposure, the cost of the fee relative to the economic exposure obtained is small. It remains small even after the proposed increase. The Exchange notes that the increase is modest relative to the value of the exposure each NDX contract provides. 2. Statutory Basis The Exchange believes that its proposal is consistent with Section 6(b) of the Act, in general, and furthers the objectives of Sections 6(b)(4) and 6(b)(5) of the Act, in particular, in that it provides for the equitable allocation of reasonable dues, fees and other charges among members and issuers and other persons using any facility, and is not designed to permit unfair discrimination between customers, issuers, brokers, or dealers. The Exchange believes that its proposal to increase the Non- Priority Customer NDX fees for regular orders from $0.75 to $1.25 per contract is reasonable because Priority Customers will continue to be assessed a lower fee as compared to Non-Priority Customers, and the existing notes and surcharges in NDX will continue to apply unchanged. The Exchange believes that, even with the increase, Non-Priority Customer pricing in NDX will remain competitive and will continue to attract order flow to the Exchange. Purpose The Exchange proposes to amend the Fund, shares of which are currently listed and traded on the Exchange pursuant to Rule 8.201-E (Non-Generic), to list and trade on the Exchange pursuant to Rule 8.201-E (Generic). The Commission approved the listing and trading of shares of the Fund (the ``Shares'') on the Exchange under Rule 8.201-E (Non-Generic) on April 19, 2022. Rule 8.201-E (Non-Generic) governs the listing and trading of Commodity-Based Trust Shares, which are securities issued by a trust (``Trust'') that holds a specified commodity, or a specified commodity and, in addition to such specified commodity, cash, that is issued by such Trust in a specified aggregate minimum number in return for a deposit of a quantity of the underlying commodity and/or cash, and that, when aggregated in the same specified minimum amount, may be redeemed by such Trust. On July 28, 2026, the Commission approved a proposed rule change to amend Rule 8.201-E (Generic). Rule 8.201-E (Generic), as amended, allows for up to 15% of a trust's net asset value (NAV) to consist of digital commodities or securities that do not independently meet the core generic eligibility criteria; adds ``digital commodity'' as a defined term; and allows for actively managed Commodity-Based Trust Shares. The Exchange proposes to now list and trade the Shares of the Fund pursuant to the generic listing standards set forth in Rule 8.201-E (Generic), as amended, which would permit the Fund to operate in reliance on the generic listing standards in Rule 8.201-E (Generic), as amended, instead of the terms of the Original Approval Order. The Exchange represents that the Shares will meet the requirements of Rule 8.201-E (Generic), as amended, on an initial and continued listing basis. In addition, the Exchange will comply with the requirements of Rule 19b-4(e) to list and trade Shares of the Fund on the Exchange. 2. Specifically, the Exchange believes the proposed rule change is consistent with the Section 6(b)(5) requirements that the rules of an exchange be designed to prevent fraudulent and manipulative acts and practices, to promote just and equitable principles of trade, to foster cooperation and coordination with persons engaged in regulating, clearing, settling, processing information with respect to, and facilitating transactions in securities, to remove impediments to and perfect the mechanism of a free and open market and a national market system, and, in general, to protect investors and the public interest. The Exchange believes the proposed rule change is designed to remove impediments to and perfect the mechanism of a free and open market and, in general, to protect investors and the public interest because it would allow the Fund to be listed and traded under Rule 8.201-E (Generic), as amended, instead of Rule 8.201-E (Non-Generic). The proposed change would permit the Fund to operate in reliance on the generic listing standards in Rule 8.201-E (Generic), as amended, instead of the terms of the Original Approval Order, thereby facilitating the listing and trading of an exchange-traded product that will enhance competition among market participants, to the benefit of investors and the marketplace. The Exchange represents that the Shares will meet the requirements of Rule 8.201-E (Generic), as amended, on an initial and continued listing basis. B. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Burden on Competition The Exchange does not believe that the proposed rule change will impose any burden on competition that is not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purpose of the Act. IV. Solicitation of Comments Interested persons are invited to submit written data, views and arguments concerning the foregoing, including whether the proposed rule change is consistent with the Act.
